evidence.claim: A winding road through goldfields, then hill crests toward Canada
evidence.quote: The Taylor Highway provides access to the historic Fortymile gold mining district. It's a narrow winding and beautiful road that joins the Top of the World Highway, which leads to Dawson City, Yukon Territory.

evidence.claim: then hill crests toward Canada
evidence.quote: along much of its length, it skirts the crest of the hills

evidence.claim: The Taylor Highway winds through the Fortymile goldfields on a narrow road with steep grades.
evidence.quote: The Taylor Highway provides access to the historic Fortymile gold mining district. It's a narrow winding and beautiful road

evidence.claim: Alaska DOT includes the Taylor and Top of the World highways in its scenic-byway program, highlighting mountain views, the Fortymile River and old mine workings.
evidence.quote: DOT&PF / DMIO / Alaska's Scenic Byways / Taylor & Top of the World Highways

evidence.claim: Leaving Tetlin Junction, the drive offers views of the Alaska Range and Mentasta Mountains.
evidence.quote: views of the Alaska Range and the Mentasta Mountains as you head out of Tetlin Junction.

evidence.claim: Wagon trails supplied Eagle, Chicken and the Fortymile Mining District in the nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: Wagon trails had supplied Eagle, Chicken, and the historic Fortymile Mining District since the nineteenth century.

evidence.claim: The Fortymile Road was established in 1951 and later renamed for Ike P. Taylor.
evidence.quote: The Fortymile Road was established in 1951 and later renamed in honor of ARC President (1932–1948) Ike P. Taylor.

evidence.claim: The Taylor Highway continues to Eagle; at Jack Wade Junction it also connects with the Top of the World Highway for seasonal road access to Dawson City.
evidence.quote: It connects to the Top of the World Highway 96 miles (154 km) from Tetlin, at Jack Wade Junction, allowing road access to Dawson City, Yukon during parts of the year.

evidence.claim: Begin at Tetlin Junction on the Alaska Highway and follow the Taylor toward Chicken.
evidence.quote: from Tetlin Junction, about 11 miles (17 km) east of Tok on the Alaska Highway, to Eagle.

evidence.claim: At Jack Wade Junction, turn east onto the Top of the World Highway toward the Canadian border.
evidence.quote: beginning at a junction with the Taylor Highway near the unincorporated community of Jack Wade, Alaska travelling east

evidence.claim: That road takes its name from its course along hill crests, with views down into the valleys.
evidence.quote: The highway is so named because, along much of its length, it skirts the crest of the hills, giving looks down on the valleys.

evidence.claim: Old mine workings mark the journey toward Boundary; beyond the border, the highway continues to West Dawson on the Yukon River.
evidence.quote: Continue on to the U.S./Canada border at Boundary, then to Dawson City, 78 miles farther. Look for old mine workings along the way.

evidence.claim: steep grades
evidence.quote: several steep, narrow grades

evidence.claim: highlighting mountain views, the Fortymile River and old mine workings.
evidence.quote: The Fortymile River system is a National Wild & Scenic River

evidence.claim: old mine workings
evidence.quote: Look for old mine workings along the way.

evidence.claim: the highway continues to West Dawson on the Yukon River.
evidence.quote: its terminus at the ferry terminal in West Dawson, Yukon, on the western banks of the Yukon River.

evidence.claim: Chicken began as a gold-mining settlement in the late nineteenth century, and mining remains part of its life.
evidence.quote: Chicken was settled by gold miners in the late-19th century.

evidence.claim: Active gold mines and inactive dredges share the area.
evidence.quote: There are still active gold mines and inactive gold dredges in this area.

evidence.claim: The Pedro Dredge gives that machinery a particular history: built in California, it was shipped to Pedro Creek north of Fairbanks in 1938.
evidence.quote: It was built by the Yuba Manufacturing Company in California, and was shipped to Pedro Creek north of Fairbanks, Alaska in 1938.

evidence.claim: After operating there until 1958, it was dismantled, trucked to Chicken and reassembled the following year.
evidence.quote:
It was assembled there, and operated until 1958.
The following year it was disassembled, trucked to Chicken, Alaska and reassembled.

evidence.claim: Its last cleanup came in October 1967; in 1998 the 500-ton dredge moved overland to Chicken Gold Camp.
evidence.quote:
until October 1967, when it produced its final cleanup.
In 1998, the 500 ton dredge was moved overland to its current location at the Chicken Gold Camp.

evidence.claim: The creek took its name from Jack Anderson and Wade Nelson, the original claim locators.
evidence.quote: The creek was named for Jack Anderson and Wade Nelson, the original locators.

evidence.claim: Its first claims date to 1892. Uncertainty over whether claims lay in Alaska or Canada led many miners to file in both Eagle and Dawson City.
evidence.quote: Because of questions as to whether claims were in Canada or Alaska, many miners filed claim locations in both Dawson City, Yukon Territory and Eagle, Alaska. Jack Wade Creek's first claims were located in 1892

evidence.claim: Jack Wade had a post office from 1901 until 1948.
evidence.quote: Jack Wade received a post office in 1901, which remained until 1948.

evidence.claim: A painted line inside the joint inspection building marks the United States–Canada border.
evidence.quote: A line painted on the floor in the building marks the US-Canada border.

evidence.claim: The two countries built the shared facility in 2001, bringing their inspectors into one building.
evidence.quote: In 2001, the US and Canada constructed a joint border inspection station, where inspectors from both countries occupy a single facility.

evidence.claim: Earlier travelers faced a different arrangement: American inspections took place in Tok, about 120 miles away, until a log cabin-style station was built at the border in 1971.
evidence.quote: the US performed border inspection services about 120 miles (190 km) away in Tok, Alaska until 1971, when it built a log cabin-style inspection station at the border.

evidence.claim: This is North America’s northernmost international border crossing, on the highway linking Chicken with Dawson.
evidence.quote: This crossing is notable for being the northernmost international border crossing in North America.

evidence.claim: on the highway linking Chicken with Dawson.
evidence.quote: located on the Top of the World Highway, which connects the communities of Dawson, Yukon, and Chicken, Alaska

evidence.claim: The highways have no winter maintenance, steep narrow grades and long gaps between services. The border crossing operates only in summer.
evidence.quote: several steep, narrow grades and long distances between services. Winter road maintenance is not provided.

evidence.claim: The border crossing operates only in summer.
evidence.quote: this border, which is only open in summer

evidence.claim: The Fortymile River system has National Wild and Scenic River status, and the Taylor Highway provides access to it.
evidence.quote: The highway also provides access to the Fortymile River National Wild and Scenic River system.

evidence.claim: The surrounding historic district includes buildings dating from the early 1900s.
evidence.quote: A portion of Chicken, with buildings from the early 1900s

evidence.claim: In 1936 the Yukon Placer Mining Company bought a bucket-line dredge at Franklin, dismantled it and hauled it by horse over the ice to Jack Wade Creek.
evidence.quote: In 1936, the bucket line dredge working at Franklin was bought, dismantled and hauled by horses over the ice to Jack Wade Creek by the Yukon Placer Mining Co., which owned the claims.

evidence.claim: In 1938, Fred Whitehead held the contract to build the small airstrip at Jack Wade Creek.
evidence.quote: In 1938, Fred Whitehead had the contract to build the small airstrip at Jack Wade Creek

evidence.claim: The Top of the World Highway continues east to a ferry terminal in West Dawson, on the Yukon River’s western bank.
evidence.quote: travelling east to its terminus at the ferry terminal in West Dawson, Yukon, on the western banks of the Yukon River.

evidence.claim: The Taylor Highway continues to Eagle
evidence.quote: extends 160 miles (258 km) from Tetlin Junction, about 11 miles (17 km) east of Tok on the Alaska Highway, to Eagle.

evidence.claim: follow the Taylor toward Chicken.
evidence.quote: Pass through the Fortymile goldfields, made famous in Jack London novels. The Fortymile River system is a National Wild & Scenic River with miles of exciting whitewater. Visit Chicken
